utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Then Madam usher, could you please escort Mr. Cengic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, may I just say that we would like to express our appreciation for the fact a lot of work went into the transcript after court yesterday to deal with the problem that I mentioned of continuous prose without identifying the speaker. And we very much appreciate that. Mr. Harmon and I have been discussing possibilities to streamline the procedure in future which is going to be mentioned, I think, in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was going to have Mr. Hannis raise the issue, but I can address it frankly right now. In respect of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should we not first start with -- Mr. Cengic is now here, and I was informed that solutions had been found, or at least that hard work had been done on it. So perhaps we first -- Mr. Cengic, good afternoon. Perhaps we first start the cross-examination of the witness. If there's any need to do it early, then we better take off five minutes at the end rather than let Mr. Cengic wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I didn't have in mind that we should deal with it. I just wanted to express my appreciation for the work that went on last night while the witness was coming into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a development of good relationship continued after court. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, good afternoon. Mr. Cengic, it's right, is it, that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of something called the initiative board of the SDS in Novi Grad, at least up to the November 1990 elections? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every political party had their own initiative boards, so he probably was. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, is it right that Mr. Krajisnik took part in two or three meetings after the November 1990 elections of the type that you described, to negotiate division and allocation of positions in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that several meetings were held, but yes, there were more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many more do you say?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if Mr. Krajisnik's recollection is two or three, you would dispute that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were about five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Five or six at which Mr. Krajisnik was present, or five or six all together?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he was at the last meetings. Now, whether he was at the first one, too, I can't say. Perhaps he wasn't at the first one. There were four or five after that. I'm not sure that he was at the first meeting. At the first meeting, I made a proposal that all power should be shared among all the parliamentary parties. Then there were representatives --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't want to go into the content of the meeting unless it's helping you to recall the answer to my question. Can we try and put it this way: You're not in a position to say with any confidence that Mr. Krajisnik attended more than two or three of those negotiating meetings, are you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assertion is that he was there at at least four meetings. Perhaps he did not attend the first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you know that he became -- perhaps you don't, but that he became president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament sometime in November 1990? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was elected to the parliament, but the constituent assembly was held after we had reached all those interparty agreements; that is to say, that at the moment when the negotiations were taking place, Mr. Krajisnik had not been elected president of the parliament yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know when Mr. Krajisnik was elected president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that during the negotiations, the talks, he had not been elected. I don't know exactly when he was elected, but it was certainly after the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if I put it to you that Mr. Krajisnik became president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly on the 18th of November 1990, you say that's wrong, do you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say anything because I cannot claim what the date was exactly when these meetings were held. But I do know for sure that at the time when the meetings were held, Mr. Krajisnik had not been elected president of the assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's get it clear, Mr. Cengic: You're not suggesting that these meetings to negotiate allocation of positions were all concluded by late November 1990, are you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were all finished before Mr. Krajisnik was elected president of the parliament of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please, let's not fence around, Mr. Cengic. I'm asking you specific dates. Are you suggesting that those negotiating -- negotiation meetings were all concluded by the 18th of November 1990?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the date of Krajisnik's election of president to the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it is your recollection, and is it possible then that the at least four meetings that you asserted took place in the course of no more than a couple of weeks?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately. The documentation, the minutes of these meetings were at Mr. Hadzic's, and he got killed. It was perhaps lost subsequently. But I did not take any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please, may I simply remind you, Mr. Cengic, that you're here giving evidence on the basis of a solemn declaration. So what you remember, you remember; and what you can't remember, please tell the Trial Chamber you can't remember. That, I do believe the Trial Chamber would endorse as a proper approach to evidence. So are we saying or are you saying, then, Mr. Cengic, that you actually don't have any clear recollection of the period over which these negotiating meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for sure that before Mr. Krajisnik's election as president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, these negotiations took place, before that. That's what I remember for sure. I did not remember the dates, and I never thought I would need the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And had been concluded before his election as president of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last meeting was held before Mr. Krajisnik was appointed president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After the elections in November 1990, would you accept Mr. Krajisnik's recollection that he hardly ever went to Novi Grad and went, in fact, before the start of the war only once to the SDS headquarters which is about 12 kilometres from Zabrdje? Would you dispute that recollection?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and this is what the doorkeeper told me, it's not that it was that way. It wasn't that way. Mr. Krajisnik was seen very often at the municipality building at the SDS offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the records that the doorkeeping service has. I did not state last time that I had seen him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your evidence yesterday, and this is page 78 of the transcript, you said in relation to this point, you said, "First of all, this is my impression that Mr. Krajisnik was very often the guest of the SDS offices in the town hall." And then you were asked by Mr. Harmon: "Was it reported to you that he appeared at the town hall by others?" And you said: "It was customary for record to be taken of anybody who wasn't an employee of the town hall entering and leaving the building, and such information should have been kept by the janitor." So you're now saying today not just that it should have been kept by the janitor, but that it was kept by the janitor and that you specifically discussed with the janitor Mr. Krajisnik's to-ings and fro-ings from that building. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not only ask about Mr. Krajisnik's entrances. After office hours, I would usually ask who came and went. I thought that Mr. Krajisnik and everybody else were equal. I was simply asking about who came and who went. It's not that I was particularly following what Mr. Krajisnik was doing, and that was not what I had targeted. Every day, I had occasion to see these records as to who came in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So yesterday when you gave this evidence, you could have -- you could have added yesterday that you'd actually seen the records of who had gone in and out of the building. But you didn't add that yesterday. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one ever asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were telling the Court it was your impression, and now today you're telling the Court that you actually saw written records, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The question that was put to Mr. Cengic yesterday, and was referred to on page 78, was: "Was it reported to you that he appeared at the town hall by others?" Not a question as to whether he saw records.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's not one of Mr. Harmon's finest interventions, Your Honour, because -- I'll continue with this questioning as far as I need to, which is not very far, I think, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Stewart put to the witness his answer about an impression he had. Since Mr. Stewart did not refer to any question, of course, you could have asked the witness in redirect any further questions on that. But I think it was more appropriate not to intervene at that moment. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I think in any case I've got to the stage where anything further would be comment rather than useful questions on this topic, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The lead negotiator in the meetings that you've described to allocate and divide functions in the municipality, the lead negotiator for the SDS was Radislav Unkovic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the first meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say the first meetings, Mr. Cengic --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also, I was not the person in charge at the first meetings. As our work progressed, some people from the different political parties gained more confidence from the others, and then they led. On behalf of the SDS, that was Mr. Krajisnik. On behalf of the SDA, it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You effectively took the lead for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who did you take over from as the lead negotiator for the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first meeting that Mr. Krajisnik attended was chaired by Mr. Mrahorovic. A lot of dividing and multiplying had to be done in order do have a fair distribution of positions. This required quite a bit of math, and Mr. Mrahorovic was not very good at this math, and the fact that I was a mathematics teacher was probably helpful, and that contributed to my prominence. Mr. Safet Hadzic authorised me on behalf of the SDA. He was present, and he gave me power on behalf of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said about Mr. Krajisnik, and this is page 15 of yesterday's transcript, you were asked by Mr. Harmon: "Can you tell us very succinctly what positions the SDS took in respect of the positions that were subject to negotiations." And you said: "Well, at the first option that Mr. Krajisnik wanted was to get more than the election results would reflect so we could not reach agreement straight away." Mr. Cengic, I suggest to you there that there was nothing in the least bit unusual about that position. That was part of the cut and thrust of the negotiating exercise you were engaged in. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said yesterday, that I did not find this unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you were asked, it was just slightly higher up the page at page 15, you were asked specifically "in the end, Mr. Cengic, were the negotiations that your delegation had with the SDS delegations successful?" You said, well, they were, they were successful. We managed to sign an agreement and distribute executive positions among these three parties. That's to say, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ." So the overall picture was that they were no doubt quite tough negotiations, but they actually worked out with a compromise which everybody signed up to. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is correct, and that's what I said yesterday, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was a contributor to and in the end a supporter of exactly that compromise, successful agreement that was reached?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had he not been in favour of this kind of agreement, he wouldn't have signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you say that you proposed, and you personally you had in mind, that the other parties who had gained votes of the elections, that's to say, outside the main three, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, that the other parties should also have positions. That's at page 11 of yesterday's transcript. And you -- that the purpose -- well, I beg your pardon. That was your personal suggestion right at the beginning, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the first meeting, that proposal was turned down. That's correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was it, in fact, supported by your own SDA colleagues?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This proposal was not discussed at all. I did not consult anybody beforehand, so I just spoke off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the picture is, then, it was your own idea which you produced there and then at the meeting, but from what you've said, it seemed that it didn't fall on fertile ground because it didn't lead on to any discussion at all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You also referred, and this is at page 16 of yesterday's transcript, to an agreement which you say Mr. Krajisnik reported to you, an agreement that you say he said he had made with Muhamed Cengic, who was at that time vice-president of the SDA, that the municipality of Novi Grad should get one more position than justified by the election results with compensation of a position in the Municipality of Cajnice. I hope I pronounced that even approximately right. You agree, that's a summary of your position, Mr. Cengic, on this point?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is correct, but I said, and that's the way it was, that someone from the SDS - it didn't have to be Krajisnik - I think that I didn't mention that it was Krajisnik who was discussing things with Muhamed Cengic, but somebody else from the SDS, that they had reached this kind of agreement at a high level, at a higher level, that they agreed on these exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may be that we can get agreement, Mr. Cengic, on this, then, because what you actually said in your evidence yesterday, and this is at page 16, you said at one point in time, Mr. Krajisnik made an offer, he said, that he had agreed with Muhamed Cengic that the Municipality of Novi Grad should get one more position and so on. But what I put to you, Mr. Cengic, is that in fact agreement had been reached between Mr. Velibor Ostojic on the one hand for the SDS and Mr. Muhamed Cengic for the SDA. Does that now sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is right, yes. Actually, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And -- but in the end, it didn't come to anything because the SDS representatives in your negotiations at your local level failed to persuade you and your colleagues to carry out any such swap of positions. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for that was that the following day, I went to talk with Mr. Muhamed Cengic, and he told me that there was no such agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you to clarify one thing which is totally unclear. The answer of the witness included one more position than merited. One more position in what exactly? Because there seems to be a swap between municipalities. It's not entirely clear to me what positions we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try and clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, this is right, is it, that - leaving aside your last answer - what was reported to you, you say, by Mr. Krajisnik was an agreement that Novi Grad should get one more position than -- the SDS, rather, should get one more position in Novi Grad in these negotiations than would otherwise be justified by the election results, and that in compensation, according to you, you were told that the SDA would get one more position in the Municipality of Cajnice. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole point was as follows -- that is, you were correct in what you're saying. But I then said how could you draw a comparison between a locality which has 100.000 voters and another locality that has less than 5.000 voters? But nevertheless, I did approach Mr. Muhamed Cengic and asked him whether there was such an agreement really, and the answer was that there was no such agreement. Now, at the next meeting, I said that there was not going to be any swapping of positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because, in fact, I put it to you that Cajnice was never mentioned by Mr. Krajisnik or anybody else in relation to any such agreement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cajnice? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That it was never mentioned? It wasn't part of --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cajnice was being offered as compensation for Novi Grad. However, of course, there was no agreement to that effect because Cajnice is a small locality. One street in Novi Grad is larger than Cajnice itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you were dealing with this point in your evidence yesterday, you said, and this is page 16, that you checked at the SDA headquarters whether there was any such agreement with regard to this kind of an exchange of mandates, and then I'm quoting. And then the next bit is now a direct quote. "But they said that the answer was no, that no such agreement was reached." So Mr. Cengic, when you were referring yesterday to "they said that the answer was no and the people you checked with at the SDA headquarters," then are you saying that according to your evidence today that actually it was Mr. Muhamed Cengic himself that you asked?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said "they," I meant in any case Muhamed Cengic. I meant the person mentioned as having had an agreement with the SDS, having signed the agreement with the SDS. I went to the staff, and that's where Muhamed Cengic was, and I talked to him. And that was the answer I got from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the difference between your evidence yesterday and the evidence today is that you specifically mention Mr. Muhamed Cengic, but, Mr. Cengic, I also put to you --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- that the difference between the evidence you have given in this hearing this week and what you said in the statement that you signed in 1998 is that in that statement, you said nothing whatever about having checked with anybody about this agreement. And I think perhaps in fairness, you should be shown this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could the witness have the B/C/S version of his statement which the rest of us have in English dated the 22nd of January 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not in evidence, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's not in evidence, Your Honour. But I'd assume that it was readily available. It has been on provisional lists for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want someone to provide it to Madam usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's you or whether it's the Prosecution. Is there a copy available? Otherwise, mine could be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's a fairly short passage, Your Honour. I just want to be fair to the witness in having him see it, but he can have that opportunity in a moment if it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The particular passage, Mr. Cengic, it's just that you -- it's in paragraph 13 - it's been numbered now - of your statement. And you say: "One day I recall Krajisnik saying that Velibor Ostojic informed him that he had just made an agreement with Muhamed Cengic," so that confirms what you said this morning -- this afternoon, rather, "to give one more leading position in the executive bodies of Novi Grad to the SDS in Novi Grad and in return give the SDA one more position in Cajnice." And then you go on. And it's just the next couple of sentences which are key here. "I didn't believe that because Cajnice is a small town with some 3.000 inhabitants. It would have seemed much more likely if they had arranged a swap between positions in Novi Grad and Banja Luka. Krajisnik's tactic didn't change anything, and we continued to assign positions as I will describe below." Mr. Cengic, what I'm suggesting to you is it's extremely surprising if, in fact, you took the clear simple step of checking this with Mr. Muhamed Cengic himself, that you didn't say exactly that when you gave your statement in 1998. Why didn't you mention it then?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was giving my statement in 1998, I didn't even think that I was going to come here and that everything would have to be stated exactly word by word. And this was a matter of establishing truth, and already four years had elapsed. It was difficult to establish how exactly things went. I only know that the agreement failed, and when I went to Muhamed Cengic, I did not really think that that was an important matter. The important matter to me was that the agreement had not been reached as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cengic, it comes to this: That in your statement that you gave in 1998, you gave your reasons for inferring that that agreement could not have taken place in those terms, instead of simply saying as a matter of fact that you had checked with one of the parties to the agreement and had been told that it hadn't, that's what I'm putting to you. That it's surprising that you go in for reasoning and inference and you now tell the Trial Chamber that you actually checked with the person involved and there was no need for reasoning and inference. That's what I'm putting to you. What do you say?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you the following: Even if Muhamed Cengic had said at the time that this matter had to be pursued, I would not have -- I would not have done so because having been responsible for Novi Grad, I would have criticised Muhamed Cengic for having discussed such important matters. I went there not because I was in a dilemma as to whether this should be implemented or not; but rather, to verify whether what Mr. Krajisnik was saying was true or not. Indeed, it would have been highly inappropriate to reach such an agreement because Muhamed Cengic was a person who could have erred in his assessment. I could not afford that, being at the municipal level and referring back to the comparison that I've already talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on, Mr. Cengic. Yesterday at page 17 of the transcript, you described how during the negotiations that took place in the municipality building, there was only a wall separating the SDA offices from the SDS offices. And you said sometimes you would go to your --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- The SDA rooms with your delegation, but more often you would stay in the hall and wait for the SDS to return. And then you said: "When we went downstairs, I heard on several occasions Mr. Krajisnik, since the walls are thin, talk to someone called Radovan or Raso." Mr. Cengic, it's not a hundred per cent clear, so I would ask you to make clear, when you talk about when you went downstairs, are you talking about -- does that mean going to the SDS rooms, or does it mean going to the hall?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corridor ran throughout the building. The negotiations took place in the room number 327. Now, when I say "downstairs," I meant that we were descending from the third to the first floor, and the SDA, SDS, and HDZ office were side by side on the first floor. That's what I meant when I said downstairs, from the third to the first floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So to put it in an absolute nutshell, when you were talking about going downstairs, you were talking about going down to those offices where there was only a wall separating the SDA and SDS rooms. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was on those occasions then that you would on several occasions you say hear Mr. Krajisnik talking to someone called Radovan or Raso?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and this was not unusual to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying that you could actually follow the conversation, or just that you pick up odd phrases and words?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my intention to eavesdrop, nor did I ever do that in my life. Simply while I was having a cup of coffee and a cigarette, I could hear this conversation going on. Of course, we would keep talking about the matters that we had to discuss. I never even thought of things happening that did happen and that ever anybody would ask me questions to that effect. If these conversations were followed, they were probably followed by the services in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the typical pattern there was that you and your colleagues were naturally talking about what you had got to talk about while there was discussion and you're presumably talking about telephone calls taking place in the room next door?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, telephone calls, right. But since I did not enter the premises, I didn't enter the offices, these could have been live conversations. I cannot say. Although the offices were one next to each other, I never entered their office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cengic, if you were not hearing sufficiently well to distinguish between a live conversation and a telephone conversation, then I suggest to you that you weren't hearing very much of these conversations at all. Do you see what I'm saying? What I'm putting to you it's terribly easy to tell the difference between a telephone conversation going on on the other side of a wall and a live, two-person conversation where the people are in the same room. It's just easy. So I'm putting it to you that you weren't able to draw that distinction, you were not really following all that closely these conversations?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not following the conversations at all. When people greet each other, they tend to speak a bit more loudly, saying hi, hello, how are you doing. And of course, that was something I did not pay any attention to, nor would I do that today. I would hear them greet each other, and then would not hear what went on in their conversation. I had no intention of eavesdropping on anyone. I merely heard someone greeting somebody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cengic, I do not know whether you understood the question rightly. But what Mr. Stewart puts to you is the following: If you are able to hear a name, then at least you should be able to hear whether one person is just speaking, waiting for an answer not given directly to him, but through a telephone, and then continue to speak just on his own. Mr. Stewart puts to you that it should be quite clear that if you are able to hear the name of the other participants in the conversation, that at least you should also hear whether that person is speaking alone, waiting for an answer, then speaking again, or whether someone else is heard to answer whatever he says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my intention was not to listen to other people's conversations. It was simply while I was entering my office, I heard this name that I mentioned being mentioned, and then I entered the office. I was not there listening to conversations. Of course, since Mr. Krajisnik was receiving a lot of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. delegations, he could have talked to many different people. I don't know what was going on behind the door. I'm just saying that on several occasions, I could hear the name Radovan or Raso mentioned, but I cannot go into any details. I wish to emphasise once again Your Honour that never in my life had I eavesdropped on anyone, nor would I wish to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the name Ostojic or Velibor being mentioned in the course of any of these conversations, conversations of Mr. Krajisnik's that you --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that so far as Mr. Krajisnik consulted anybody else in relation to these negotiations, that the person that he consulted first or most would normally have been Mr. Ostojic? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know it? I wouldn't even know if I was downstairs or in the offices. No, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Thank you, Mr. Cengic. Different issue, then, this proposal for a separate Zabrdje commune, just to identify the topic because we're moving on, it's right, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik was not involved in that process, that project, that idea at all, was he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never said that he did participate in that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So what I just put to you is correct: He wasn't involved in that process, project, idea at all? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know? I know for a fact that Boro Bjelica came and said that they were going to establish a local commune. Whether Mr. Krajisnik was abreast of what Boro Bjelica was saying and in view of the fact that his house was in Zabrdje and in view of his influence, I don't think anything could have happened without his knowledge. But Mr. Krajisnik did not appear at these meetings in person to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You described, and this is at page 40 of yesterday's transcript, you described a meeting that you held in July 1991, you say, in an attempt to resolve this problem, you were asked: "Did you call Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik to assist you?" Now, Mr. Cengic, the position is this, isn't it, there was a meeting between and you Mr. Krajisnik - that's acknowledged - around that time. But the meeting was at Mr. Krajisnik's request specifically to deal with the question of legalisation of the construction of his house. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The meeting was convened at my request. I invited them to my office. Prior to that, I thought that Mr. Krajisnik was not aware of that problem at all. When I started presenting the problem, I realised that Mr. Krajisnik was familiar with the matter. We did not talk about this problem for a long time at all because simply Mr. Krajisnik changed the topic and starting dealing with this other issue. When we're talking about the request contained in that document by Bjelica, then he sees the opportunity of being there at the municipality, and he asked me to call a lady professional dealing with the legalisation of buildings, and she was doing her job very properly. She was a daughter of the chief of the Novi Grad police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, she was the wife of the chief of Novi Grad's police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She came downstairs, and she explained to Mr. Krajisnik how much he had to pay for the legalisation of the house. He smiled and said, well, this is a very hefty amount. I won't be able to pay that amount, and let alone the others. How are they going to pay such amounts? As for the issue of the local commune, nothing was resolved. The situation remained as before except for the fact that on that occasion I saw for myself that Mr. Krajisnik was as informed about it as I was, that he knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we've already established, Mr. Cengic, there's a clear difference between your recollection and Mr. Krajisnik's as to who requested the meeting and why it was called. So we won't go over that ground again. Do you agree, then, that any discussion of any other issues apart from Mr. Krajisnik's house was very short and in the end rather incidental to the discussion that took place between you and him on that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to go back to this other issue. I would like Your Honours to see an interview given by Mr. Krajisnik for Novogradsko Oko where it says that I had come to Novi Grad upon the invitation of Cengic, and that's what confirms what I said, that it was upon my invitation that he came there. So I think you were discussing that paper already. You could take a look at it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'm sure Mr. Harmon can handle the Prosecution case, if we just confine ourselves to questions and answers in the course of your giving evidence. The -- you said in your evidence yesterday, page 41, about this meeting, "we did not talk about it that much," it being the question of Zabrdje. "We did not talk about it that much."

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you said also that he supported -- in a way, he supported the sponsors of that proposal. Mr. Cengic, if you had asked him specifically to come to a meeting to discuss this issue, it's a bit strange, isn't it, that you didn't even talk about it that much and that the most you can say is in a way he supported the sponsors?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that his position was identical to that of the proposing party, the party that proposed the idea. What else was there to infer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who were the sponsors of that proposal, to use, well, your phrase as it comes across in English?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the proposal of Bjelica. I did not see the petition. I didn't see the citizens either. I just saw Boro Bjelica, who submitted this request in writing, and he said that there are 400 signatures. I never saw these signatures. I mean...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik never suggested to you anything to be done in any context, other than according to proper law and procedures, did he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik knew how to speak very nicely. I noticed one word in the interview. He used the word "violence" in the conversation, and I never thought of violence being a way of attaining any objectives. We had to act in accordance with law and order. And he knew in advance that the proposal did not meet all the requirements set forth by the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you about that, so I might as well ask you now: Your reference to his use of the word violence is to the article in Novogradsko Oko, which was dealt with particularly at page 43 of the transcript yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We noticed, Mr. Cengic, as it happens that there appears to be an interview or an article relating to an interview with you in the same issue of that publication which -- we don't have the complete issue, but do you remember that, that there is also in the very same issue an article relating to you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a long interview. On the second, third page of that newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't suppose you happen to have it with you, do you, Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe. Maybe I do have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You have it here. Wonderful. Where is it, Mr. Cengic, then?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either here or the hotel. But it's in The Hague for sure. I don't know if I put it in my bag this morning. I mean, whether I put this newspaper into my bag this morning, but I did bring the newspaper along just in case. During the break, I'll check whether I have it right here. There is a high degree of probability that it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, it was just a transcript point that I think we'll leave to sort out in a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cengic. I would be grateful if I might ask through the Trial Chamber, Your Honour, if Mr. Cengic could make that check during the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it would not be here, Mr. Cengic, how much time would you need to get it from your hotel room approximately, if you would not have it here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think 10 or 15 minutes at the most, if a car is provided to me. I'd need 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you be willing to give up part of the time you are entitled to for a break to spend that on going to your hotel, if needed, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the truth. I came here to tell the truth. I took an oath that I would tell the truth, so by all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much. Could I ask you, Mr. Registrar, to be the point where the victims and witness section, to be the point where Mr. Cengic report whether the newspaper article is here or whether he has to fetch it from his hotel room. Yes. If you would please prepare that. Mr. Stewart, have you finished with -- well, at least, this part of the newspaper we have at this moment on our desk?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, I haven't, Your Honour. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The witness has raised this question, so I jumped forward to deal with this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In relation to the article about the interview with Mr. Krajisnik for the moment, you had referred -- or I think Mr. Harmon in his question actually referred to the last paragraph in the English translation which was Mr. Krajisnik quoted as saying, "I promised to Ismet Cengic that I would do everything to prevent the use of violence and to make sure that changes are carried out as determined by the constitution and according to the decision of the municipality." I just want to get clear, Mr. Cengic, are you suggesting that Mr. Krajisnik in some way was stirring up thoughts and fears of violence that weren't already there in the air?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One and the same thing in my opinion. After all of what happened, my opinion is different in terms of what -- compared to what I thought then. I thought then that there would be no violence. As a matter of fact, in that article when I read it, when it was published before the war, I didn't even notice the word. I did not find it striking in any way. However, after all the violence that did happen, the word gained in importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm really putting to you, Mr. Cengic, is this: I believe I'm entitled to ask this, that if you are going to say something like that about Mr. Krajisnik, it shouldn't be by innuendo. So I'm inviting to make very clear whether you are or aren't saying that Mr. Krajisnik was in any way, in any way, stirring up thoughts or feelings of violence or fears of violence that weren't already there in the air in February 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a time when intensive negotiations were still taking place. I didn't say anything. I just said that I noticed that he used the word violence. I was not saying that he was trying to promote violence in any way. I just said that he used the word. We can have a look at the newspaper itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, what it comes to is this: If your evidence comes to no more than drawing attention to the word violence in the text of the article, then, with the greatest of respect, I'm not trying to be funny or insulting, Mr. Cengic, the Trial Chamber can read the article for themselves. Anybody can read the article themselves. So I'm inviting to tell the Trial Chamber whether you're evidence -- you're proposing to add anything to the simple fact that we can read that in that newspaper?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have nothing to add except for the fact that later on, there was violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll add this question, Mr. Cengic, because I do questions and you do answers. That's the deal. That Mr. Cengic, in February 1992, you would -- nobody could have failed to know that there was the potential for violence in the air in Bosnia and Herzegovina, could they?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991? Are you talking about 1991 or 1992? Which year? 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: February 1992.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, 1992. Well, Croatia's not far away. Croatia's not far away. Dubrovnik is not far away. Vukovar is not far away from Bosnia. Every day on the news, we heard about what was going on there, and we saw what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Cengic, you correctly point out the obvious geographical fact that Croatia's not very far away. It wasn't very far away in 1991, and of course we know there was violence within Yugoslavia from well back into 1991, wasn't there? That's serious violence. Mr. Cengic, I'm suggesting we don't need to dwell on this. The answer is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And is it right just to confirm, then, Mr. Krajisnik never made any suggestion that you heard to you or that you heard or you're aware of, never any suggestion before the outbreak of the war that anything should be done according to proper law and procedures? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mr. Krajisnik that time when we had those discussions. And when I went to the republican parliament as a guest, then we would see each other the way I'm watching you now. Sometimes we would exchange greetings, too. In passing, we would nod at each other. We're from the same municipality. And there were different levels of government involved, so we did not really meet. Everybody dealt with their own problems at the level of government that they were at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I want to ask you, Mr. Cengic, in your statement it was -- it's the same statement, again, it's a relatively short passage that I'm going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I hope you allow me because otherwise we might lose track. I've one question for the witness at this moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Earlier, you said that the interview with Mr. Krajisnik confirmed that he came to you, that he even, as you said it, "I had come" - and these were the words according to you in the interview spoken by Mr. Krajisnik - "I had come to Novi Grad upon the invitation of Mr. Cengic." Could you please -- could the witness be presented with P388, and could you point exactly to that part of the interview. It's the second page -- no, it's the last page, the second of the B/C/S version. Yes, next one. Next -- yes, this one. Yes. That's fine. Mr. Cengic, could you tell me where exactly you read that Mr. Krajisnik invited you to come -- that at least Mr. Krajisnik says that he was invited by you to come to Novi Grad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this section where my name is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please read that slowly. Is that the part where it starts Ismet Cengic...? Could you please read that slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. "Ismet Cengic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Novi Grad, sought the assistance of Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who is also a person who lives in Zabrdje, in order to resolve this problem."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand that requesting the assistance, you understood that to be "invited Mr. Krajisnik to come to"? I'm just trying to find out what exactly you used as a basis for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cengic, it's slightly artificial to express this as a question, but you see, don't you, that that particular part of the interview is, in fact, the journalist's words and not a quote from Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an article written by a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was taking you, Mr. Cengic, to your statement that you gave in 1998, January 1998. You described -- it's in paragraph 27. It's a fairly short passage again. You say: "As regards the TO, Territorial Defence, when I first took office as president of the municipality, the head of the TO was a Captain Osman Dzamalija. In May 1991, the SDS suggested their candidate for this position, but his rank was lower than Dzamalija's. The Sarajevo TO command had to approve the nomination of a new TO head, and they refused the SDS candidate. They reported that they were quite satisfied with the captain and that they didn't intend to change him. Then the SDS started to pressure TO command in Sarajevo for their man. I recall that sometime in September 1991, I received a document from the TO headquarters in Sarajevo that they were prepared to accept the SDS candidate. I filed that letter away deep in my desk. The war in Croatia was going on at that time, and I wanted to keep Dzamalija in place. The SDS learned, however, that I had received authorisation to confirm the nomination of their man, and they pressured me to show them that document. As a result, the SDS man was finally appointed." Now, that's the entire passage that I've read. Do you agree, Mr. Cengic, that was obviously and grossly improper conduct on your part to have filed the letter away, as you did?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in that sense that I wouldn't give it. The assembly was supposed to appoint a commander. There was a standstill in the work of the assembly. In order to prevent anyone from getting this document, in order to prevent the document from going missing, the assembly was supposed to meet every month. And sometimes we would meet a few times a month, and we could not agree on an agenda. And that's why I put it aside so that no one could find it or so that the document would not go missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cengic, can we be clear which of those two very different things it is. You've referred to filing it away so the document would not go missing. Can we be clear first of all whether you are or are not saying that you put the document deep in your desk for safekeeping so that there was no risk of it disappearing or falling into the wrong hands? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assembly that was held in February elected Mr. Guzina according to the proposal that was made. So if I had the intention of hiding that document, I never had to show it ever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That doesn't answer my question at all, Mr. Cengic. I'm asking you either to confirm or eliminate one possibility which you have raised, which is that you put the document away, filed it deep in your desk to - I'm paraphrasing here - but to keep it safe, to prevent it from disappearing or falling into the wrong hands. Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For safekeeping, in order to keep the proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm asking questions, Mr. Cengic. Are you saying that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to keep it, and it was kept safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, in your own statement that you signed in 1998, you make it clear that you filed that letter away to hide it so that other people wouldn't see it so that you would be able to stop the change in head of the TO. That's why you did it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the TO at that moment did not represent anything in view of the fact that the Territorial Defence was directly subordinated to the Yugoslav People's Army. So it was nothing. It didn't mean a thing. They didn't have weapons except that it had its own members, but only on paper. Before that, the JNA had taken over all the weapons of the Territorial Defence. Command was taken over by the JNA, too. The head of the TO was a person who was only a formal commander of some Territorial Defence without weapons, without any kind of weapons. They didn't even have infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, in your own statement, you said: "The war in Croatia was going on at that time, and I wanted to keep Dzamalija in place." So whatever you just said, the position and Mr. Dzamalija in your eyes was sufficiently significant for you to want to take active steps to prevent his replacement. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From August until the present day, not a single session of the municipal assembly was held. So there could not have been any replacement. A decision would have to be made in order to have the replacement take place. Several sessions were scheduled. They would go on for an entire day, and nevertheless the agenda would not be agreed upon. I remember well in November and December that the European Monitors were there and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'll stop you here. Your statement reads: "I filed that letter away deep in my desk. The war in Croatia was going on at that time, and I wanted to keep Dzamalija in place. The SDS learned, however, that I had received authorisation to confirm the nomination of their man, and they pressured me to show them that document. As a result, the SDS man was finally appointed." This statement gives a firm impression that you did not want to show the authorisation to the SDS since you were afraid that it could result in the replacement of Mr. Dzamalija. Is that a correct impression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My assessment was that it was premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you keep the document away because at that time you thought the replacement of Mr. Dzamalija was not -- it was not the right moment to have him replaced and that you were therefore opposing against his replacement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both. In order for it to be kept safely and that the replacement take place in due time. I refused mobilisation then of the unit that was supposed to be sent to Dubrovnik, the tank unit that was supposed to go against Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is putting a letter somewhere in the bottom of your desk the normal procedure for dealing with letters you received? Or should they have been filed and registered in the ordinary way? Whatever the reasons were there, whether they were good or less good reasons to do that, is this against normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was an exceptional point in time. It was hard for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether you had good reasons or not, the question was whether it was the ordinary procedure that letters you received --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your view that it was premature, Mr. Cengic, the right and proper and responsible course in your position was for the matter to be discussed in the correct political processes by all the interested parties and for you to argue for your point of view and then see whether your point of view prevailed or not according to the proper democratic process. That's correct, isn't it? You agree?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be -- that finishes that line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a quarter to 4.00. Mr. Cengic, you're invited to look whether the other part of the newspaper is with you in this building, and otherwise, I take it that preparations have been made to transport you to your hotel in such a way that the newspaper article would be there. Would it be possible to make a copy already? Otherwise I foresee that the newspaper is travelling through this courtroom five or six times. Yes, I see that you are nodding yes, Mr. Registrar. We adjourn until a quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As Your Honour may be aware, you may already have the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see that there's something on our desk at this moment. You said something about -- here we have the original. Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm, of course, entirely dependent on Ms. Cmeric and Mr. Krajisnik to tell me whether there's anything of any interest in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, seriously what's happening, Ms. Cmeric and Mr. Krajisnik are reading it, so by the time I finish my few remaining questions, I should know whether there's anything arising from this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness brought it. I can imagine he would like to keep the original. If you would like to inspect whether this is a copy from the original, then it's available to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I don't suppose there will be any need to trouble the witness to leave the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that the Prosecution would also agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May we just check it, then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you would give it to the parties. And Madam usher, if at the same time -- not at the same time, but if you could subsequently escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that would be beyond the skills even of our ushers, Your Honour, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I do understand you didn't even have to travel to produce -- to bring us the -- a copy of the newspaper we discussed before. It's now -- the parties will inspect it, and whether there will be any questions about it, we'll hear that later. But Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, thank you for bringing the newspaper. In that same statement that I was referring to a few minutes ago, the one that you signed in 1998, a different paragraph altogether, I've finished with that point on paragraph 27. What's number 35, it's the last paragraph on page 5, it's about a dozen lines, but I better give it to you. You said: "In August 1991, somewhere around the 17th, I was in Croatia on holiday when my deputy called me and told me that somebody from the State Secretariat for Territorial Defence had called from Belgrade asking to come pay an official visit to the municipality. I cut my holiday short and returned to Sarajevo. We had a meeting with the officials who came from Belgrade, four colonels from the JNA. They came with a request to completely take over the secretariat of national defence and put it under the control of the JNA. They wanted all documentation. Suad Berbic was present at that meeting as well as Milosevic. The proposal these colonels made was a verbal one. I told them that when they brought me a written document from the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then I would entertain their request. They left. They really needed that documentation if they wanted to call up army and reservists for the war in Croatia. And the government had already decided that we were not to respond to such a call. We removed the secretariat for national defence documentation from the municipality office where we stored it in a safe place. They needed that documentation to be able to call up soldiers." Now, first of all, Mr. Cengic, when you say "the government had already decided that we were not to respond to such a call," the government being talked about there is the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the "we" that were not to respond to such a call, who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain whether it was the government or the Presidency, but I definitely referred to a higher level, not perhaps the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina but I meant at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's going back to the previous question. I moved on to the question, to the next bit that "we were" not to respond to such a call, to ask you just make clear who you mean there by "we."

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in June 1991, the highest level of authority, whether the Presidency or the government, I'm not sure which one, issued a decree to the effect that military conscripts and reservists should no longer be assigned to the JNA. I abided by that decree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So "we" was everybody, was it, who was liable to call-up in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever it was who respected the legally elected authority in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the legally elected government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then when you say that you removed this documentation to store it in a safe place, the purpose here was to throw an obstacle in the way of implementation of the call-up, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. By the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was the justification for your action that you took the view that the call-up was illegal?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My immediate superiors in the authority I respected, which were the authorities, and these were the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the presidency and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What you say, Mr. Cengic, that you were ordered to remove this documentation and store it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The recommendation was that documentation should be safely stored because at that time the SDS had, together with the JNA, forcibly taken away the documentation, such documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could the witness have Exhibit P390, please, 3-9-0.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said something. Could you say it so loud that it can be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am familiar with this matter, with this letter sent to me by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You saw this letter yesterday, so I don't want to go all through it. But the particular complaints that are listed there towards the bottom of the page, by this we mean primarily, and then it says the first dash: "Unauthorised and illegal removement of military documentation and direct violation of federal laws and other regulations; failure to initiate procedure to relieve of duty the municipal secretary for national defence and his deputy; failure to implement the conclusions of the executive board regarding the analysis of unlawful housing construction in our municipality; and making possible the further unlawful building of houses." And then: "Failure to put on the agenda the citizens' initiative to separate and establish the local commune of Rajlovac." And it was correct, wasn't it, Mr. Cengic, that whatever your own personal justifications for doing it, there was substance in all these charges, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. Not in a single one of these. Because our children, our army, and our reservists were sent by the JNA to the battle front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Cengic, I'm going to have to invite you perhaps explain what the point is in your last answer.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day, coffins carrying dead soldiers arrived in our area. These were people who were killed at the front in Croatia and were called up by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So your position is that you were -- is this fair, that you were, if you like, conscientiously entitled to obstruct call-up and obstruct men going to the Croatian front?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I not had the -- this possibility allowed for by the law, I would not have done that because the position of our government, of the presidency, was not to send recruits to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on, Mr. Cengic. In your evidence yesterday, and this is at page 87 of the transcript, you were asked by Mr. Harmon where you would rank Mr. Krajisnik in the hierarchy of the Bosnian Serb leadership. And you gave an answer that in your opinion and the opinion of your friends, Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic were at the same level within this hierarchy, whereas all the others are far away from them in the line, far down the line. No date was put on either question or answer. Does your assessment there of the position of Mr. Krajisnik and Dr. Karadzic for that matter in the hierarchy, does that relate to the whole period through to post-Dayton, in other words, 1996?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the Dayton Accords, Mr. Karadzic was not part of the authorities. He was just president of the SDS. Whereas Mr. Krajisnik was president of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. As for Novi Grad, in view of the fact that Mr. Krajisnik lived in the area of Novi Grad, a far greater influence was wielded in Novi Grad by Mr. Krajisnik. And keeping in mind this entire situation, I stated that he was there at the top in terms of the hierarchy. I never had occasion to hear that Karadzic ever came to the territory of the Novi Grad Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said that before the Dayton Accord, Mr. Karadzic was just president of the SDS. Do you know of any other positions held by Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the aggression, prior to the war. Prior to the outbreak of the war. And then later on, I cannot say which were the functions that Mr. Karadzic exercised in Republika Srpska. It seems to me that he was the president, but no elections were held. I don't know how that came to pass. I only know what the substance of the 1990 elections was. Karadzic was not on any of the lists at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know of any other positions held by Mr. Krajisnik apart from president of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, and then also subsequently the Serb Assembly and Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he was a member of the presidency, of that first presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where would you place -- not now, of course, but where would you place Dr. Nikola Koljevic in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the presidency but was not held high. He was not highly esteemed by the people as a politician.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He's one of the ones who's far away from Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic in the line; he was far down the line, was he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, but that does not necessarily have to be true for the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What about Dr. Plavsic? Where would you place her in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between Karadzic and Krajisnik, who were on one and the same level, and she would then be second, although a bit further down, but above Koljevic. Somewhere at Mladic's level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What presidency do you say Dr. Koljevic was a member of?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Koljevic was a member of the state presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected in the 1990 elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You said in your evidence yesterday, and this is at page 89. Well, it starts at page 88 actually. You described a meeting that you'd had with a delegation, representatives of the Serb community, from Rajlovac, and that meeting you said was on the 26th of February 1996. So it was shortly post-Dayton. And you said that --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I meant -- that is to say, the meeting took place three days before the integration, the Rajlovac meeting. Before -- that is to say, before the integration meaning the integration at Rajlovac, not the Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you gave a specific date, the 26th of February 1996. You're sticking with that date, are you?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 26th of February 1996, that was the day of integration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see. Right. That's simple. So at the foot of page 87 --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I had that meeting three days earlier. I happen to have here with me an excerpt from the papers about that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say "the papers," what papers do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oslobodjenje. I'm not sure whether it's Oslobodjenje or Vecernje Novine because I used to store all the clippings from the papers that talked about me or the municipality because I had this idea of writing a book that would relate to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say you've got it with you, do we mean again back at your hotel, in your bag, in your pocket?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Here in the building?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building. I have something in my pockets as well. Although my pockets are quite small, I do have something there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You certainly come supplied, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have another interview published in the Oko newspaper. Perhaps it would be a good idea for me to say that this paper, the paper that we referred to earlier, was privately owned by Janis Tadic, a Croat. The editor-in-chief was a Bosniak, and the general manager was a Serb. The board of editors was in the same building where Mojmilo was. It was destroyed later on. They published a wartime edition. I think there were editions 1 and 2. I have a part of it here. Perhaps for the purposes of truth, it would not be a bad idea to photocopy this as well, as part of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, if it's just two copies of wartime publications, that as such doesn't make it relevant yet because we're not here writing the history of the war, but we're hearing a case. If you would however, give an opportunity to the parties to look at it, they always could decide that it is relevant or is not relevant for them. And now I see that the Defence is in an advantageous position at this very moment. So if you would give it to Madam usher, and perhaps first give it to the Defence so that it could be read. And I leave it to the parties whether there's any relevance in those documents he has. I see that you're coming --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cengic, first of all, the sound of the paper prevents the interpreters from hearing what we are saying. If you would not mind to leave it for inspection if the parties would like to see it, that would be good. But at this moment, spontaneous reading out of these documents is not something the parties have asked for and not something the Chamber would decide that it was proper to do. Nevertheless, the Chamber appreciates your most willingness to contribute to our finding of the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder whether the witness will start producing them from behind his ear. I may have started to worry. Your Honour, from a practical point of view, may I simply ask this through the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, are you leaving The Hague today, or are you going to be staying overnight?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not in charge of my comings and goings. You'll have to ask the people who invited me to come here. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All I had in mind, Your Honour, was of course if something does come up, and then we did -- it doesn't seem at all likely, but if Mr. Cengic were at least still in The Hague, that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be wise to ask Mr. Cengic to leave whatever he has and don't confuse magic with the administration of justice, Mr. Stewart, that whatever he would have, that he gives it to the Registry, that copies are made, and that the parties could have look at it and find out whether there is any relevance in it. And since I do not expect Mr. Cengic to leave this evening, there might be a possibility to ring a bell and see whether it would be of any use to ask Mr. Cengic to stay. But that's not my starting point. Mr. Cengic, usually the parties know exactly what they would like to ask from a witness. But you come with your own initiative. And as I said, it's highly appreciated. Would it be possible to leave the originals so that they can be copied over the next break and that the parties could have a look at it and see whether they find it useful or not to ask any questions about it. Would you be willing to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I brought it here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a newspaper article, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a couple of paragraphs. It's quite a short article. We supplied copies in Serbian to the interpreters. It's from Glas Srpska, 23rd of January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what I'm going to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I need a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry. I hoped and thought that was being provided right now. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They did cost only one and a half dinar, Mr. Harmon, so I take it that...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
