utterances.text: If Mr. Harmon's Serbian is like mine, it will be worth every dinar to him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'm going to invite you to read two particular paragraphs, but of course I'm not preventing you -- I wish to read through the intermediate paragraphs as well so that you're happy with the context. Would you read, please, the very first paragraph, it says Sarajevo, 22nd January. The first paragraph, if you wouldn't mind reading, that then that can be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry. I meant read aloud. I beg your pardon, Mr. Cengic. If you read it aloud, our interpreters do wonders, but they need it to be read aloud.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although it's written in Cyrillic, I know Cyrillic. There would be other people who would ask for it to be rewritten in another language. But fortunately, I know this. "The President of the Republican Assembly of Republika Srpska, Momcilo Krajisnik, addressed an appeal today to the population of Serb Sarajevo not to move out, and he called upon those who had already left to come back." That's the section you meant, right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And then I'd invite you to read to yourself the next few paragraphs, but then read out loud if you would the last paragraph in the third column.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already read that, and now I'm going to read this to you. "I appeal to the Serb people to remain at their homes, and I call upon those who had already left to come back so that we can build our Sarajevo together." That is what the president of the NS RS said. Oh, is it New Sarajevo or is it Republika Srpska? I don't know what NS is. NS is the abbreviation I see here. Do you want me to go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We suggest that NS means "People's Assembly." Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. Since he was president of the assembly, yes. "Our policy has not changed at all, and we enter the" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's all right, Mr. Cengic. I just want to ask you, do you remember such public pronouncements being reported from Mr. Krajisnik in early 1996 of this nature?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the newspapers that were published in Sarajevo, I did not have the opportunity of seeing this kind of thing. In all fairness, I did not buy all newspapers, and they didn't come out that often. However, in this period of time, I certainly did not have that kind of opportunity. Some of these newspapers are here, too, but this particular position of Mr. Krajisnik was never mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You also gave some evidence on what you had heard through the media, through the public media, of Mr. Krajisnik's views as to multiethnic life was the way it was put. And at paragraph -- I'm sorry, it was at page 90 of the transcript. But -- you were asked about this. You have said nothing about any private statements by Mr. Krajisnik made to you or anything said in any meeting where you were present with Mr. Krajisnik. Can we take it that Mr. Krajisnik never did express in your presence any views about multiethnic life in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already pointed out that I had only that one meeting with Mr. Krajisnik in connection with resolving the problem of the local commune of Rajlovac. We had no other meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it follows, you would agree then, that everything that you ever heard directly or indirectly from Mr. Krajisnik in relation to multiethnic life is -- was through some public outlet in some public way?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- mentioned Mr. Krajisnik's anger at the Dayton Agreement, that he expressed anger at the fact that the agreement had been signed. He was, do you remember he was angry and frustrated at what he saw as the giving up of Sarajevo to the Muslim community, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I might have just a minute. I don't think I will need a longer break, but just briefly to consult Ms. Cmeric the article which we were handed after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we first ask the -- do you want to tender this document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would then have number... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Defence Exhibit D32, the newspaper article from Glas Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that we receive a translation of the whole of the article, Mr. Stewart, because I see that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour. We will arrange that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although I do not read any Cyrillic, I see that Dayton is mentioned and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Sarajevo is mentioned. So there seems to be a context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll take care of it, Your Honour. We should have the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, if it would be helpful - it certainly would be helpful to me - if this whole article could be read. It's not a very long article, and in order to properly examine the witness about a piece of evidence that's tendered before the witness leaves. It's still a possibility today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that Mr. Stewart agrees with you by nodding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. It's entirely in Your Honours' hands whether the witness reads it or whether Ms. Cmeric is asked, for example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric might be well equipped to know what the speed of the interpreters is. So we would like to invite Ms. Cmeric to read the whole of the article of which you just read parts, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I invite Ms. Cmeric to read from the top of the article including the article, the date, line, et cetera, because that's also something that I do not read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you start reading just from the top, the name of Mr. Krajisnik is one of the first that's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: I will start from the very top of the page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CMERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "A daily newspaper of Republika Srpska. Glas Srpski, Banja Luka. Tuesday, the 23rd of January 1996. Number 7877. Year, illegible. LII, I believe. Price, 1 and a half dinars. "Appeal of Momcilo Krajisnik, President of the Assembly of the RS." The headline is: "Stay, so we can build our Sarajevo." Subheading: "We enter the forthcoming period with much more optimism and hope that the injustice done in Dayton can be redressed, says Momcilo Krajisnik. "Sarajevo, the 22nd of January (Crna). "The President of the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska, Momcilo Krajisnik, addressed an appeal today to the population of Serb Sarajevo not to move out and called upon all of those who had already left to return. `Many things have already been achieved the way we had planned them, and have had a pacifying effect on the Sarajevo Serbs.' That was Krajisnik's assessment at today's session of the staff for the implementation of the Dayton Agreement in Serb Sarajevo held in Vogosca. He pointed out that `in the latest talks, the representatives of the international community have been promising a great deal, not because they understand the Serb position, but because concrete moves have to be made'. And he expressed the hope that these talks would soon yield visible results. "`I think that this solution will be quite good and that it will have a positive effect on the Serbs in Serb Sarajevo, and that it will contribute to the return of many people who left this area,' President Krajisnik pointed out. In his view, the Serbs in Serb Sarajevo 'have prospects for the future and have no reason to move out or to be afraid.' 'I appeal to the Serb people to remain at their homes, and I call upon those who have already left to return so that we can build our Sarajevo together,' said the President of NS RS, and then added, `nothing has changed in our policy, and we enter the coming period with much more optimism and hope that the injustice done in Dayton can be redressed.' "From the session held in Vogosca today, an appeal was addressed to professional people who had left the area and who were scarce to begin with to return as soon as possible to work. The staff also looked at the problems of supply and maintaining law and order in the area of Serb Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? May I give you the right answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The right answer to what exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To what question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, if you would like to add anything, Mr. Stewart, are there any questions -- further questions in relation to this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll allow the witness who wants to -- who has listened to the whole of the text, whatever you would like to say about it, please go ahead, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I read this, I did not go to the very core of the matter. Reference is made to Serb Sarajevo all the time, not Rajlovac and what is supposed to belong to the federation. So that has to be borne in mind. There's a part of Republika Srpska that was no longer Republika Srpska, so this was an appeal to Serbs in Republika Srpska not to move out, not to Serbs in the federation, if I understand this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just give us one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your statement that you signed in 1998, and this was paragraph 43, it's a very short paragraph, Mr. Cengic, it's the penultimate paragraph on page 6, you just referred to the date Friday, April the 3rd when Mr. Milosevic, that's the local Mr. Milosevic, of course, came to your office and said, "see you after the war," took a car and left and you never saw him again. And then you say, SDS deputies and municipality employees continued to come to work, but some of them that I had contact with began to come to work wearing firearms." In fact, you turned up yourself for work at that date carrying a gun, didn't you, Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. After a meeting -- of course, some SDS officials came. My secretary did not come, and he said that he was sick and therefore he could not come. Mr. Milosevic came on Friday, and he said "see you after the war." I could not believe that a war would actually happen. There were some excesses, but I was hoping that reason would prevail and that there wouldn't be a war. When I was at one of the meetings of the executive board, I don't know whether this was an accident or not, but one of the members of the executive board moved his jacket this way, and I saw guns on both sides. I can tell you that in response to that, I brought a gun along to our next meeting. But it bothered me, and that was the only time I did it. It's heavy. It's a heavy thing, a gun, to carry around like that. And anyway, if shells start falling, a gun cannot be much protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'd just like to return for a moment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I'd just like you to return for a moment to that article from Glas Srpska that we were looking at a few moments ago where I asked you to read a couple of paragraphs. It was D -- whatever it now is. I wonder if you could just read out for us again, please, the top paragraph of the last column, it's to the left of the photograph, immediately to the left of Mr. Krajisnik's photograph, the top paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Nothing has changed in our policy, and we enter the coming period with much more optimism and hope that the injustice done in Dayton can be redressed."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what -- do you understand what is being referred to there by the "injustice done in Dayton"?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the gentleman meant -- well, injustice, I mean there is no doubt about that. Both sides can talk about injustice. This is an agreement that was reached, nevertheless, and that has to be observed. But I think that Mr. Krajisnik meant that it can be redressed by way of the compensation of that part of Dobrinje that had not been reintegrated in that period. It was reintegrated only later on. Of course, I cannot make any assertions. I can't say it's actually that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I see. So you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I won't pursue this any further with the witness, Your Honour. Yes, I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you have some questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do have some questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put them before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, the Defence exhibit that is before you, I hope it is still before you, D32, the article in Cyrillic. If it's not, if could be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam usher, could you... ?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I understand this article, and I was trying to take notes as quickly as I could, this article is dated the 23rd of January 1996. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This article was published a little bit more than a month before the meeting you had with the Serb representatives from Rajlovac at which time the Serb representatives from Rajlovac told you that they had been ordered by Krajisnik to move out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As I listened to the translation of this article, I noted the following, and you can help us perhaps. What I wrote down was "Momcilo Krajisnik addressed an appeal to the population of Serb Sarajevo." What is "Serb Sarajevo"? Can you enlighten us as to what that means in terms of the geographical configuration of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know that according to the Dayton Peace Agreement, Sarajevo was divided into two parts. One part belonged to the federation and the other part to Republika Srpska. The part that was allocated to Republika Srpska is Serb Sarajevo. And that is a part that has a border with the area that belongs to the federation, and the border is Dobrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is this --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And further on, the other parts of other municipalities that were outside the nucleus of Sarajevo, that is Pale, part of the Stari Grad Municipality, Novo Sarajevo - New Sarajevo - part of the centre and so on. As for the nucleus of the town itself, the Municipality of Novi Grad was allocated to the Serb part. Parts 1 and 4. And that is where the Dayton boundary ran. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So is this an appeal by Mr. Krajisnik to the people who -- the Serbs within Serb Sarajevo not to move out, such as -- not to move out to the federation --

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Precisely. Precisely. Serbs from the part of the federation -- I mean, I'm describing it now. Grbavica, Novo Sarajevo, then Nedzarici, then Dobrosevici, Atovici, and Reljevo, Rajlovac, they belonged to the federation from then on. In the other part, there were Serbs who were in the part where Republika Srpska was, and they started moving out. So this is an appeal addressed to Serbs who started moving out from the part that was Republika Srpska. This was not an appeal to the Serbs in the part that was supposed to belong to the federation. Now, that's exactly what it says here, appeal to the population of Serb Sarajevo, that's what it says. This part exists even now. It's not called Serb Sarajevo any longer, but it is still that territory. It's called Eastern Sarajevo now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The population -- the Serb population from Rajlovac that you met with in late February were Serbs who resided in the federation portion of Sarajevo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area that under the Dayton Agreement was part of the federation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got one or two questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there any Serbs that had fled prior or during the war to Republika Srpska and had returned to the Rajlovac federal territory after the war?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with anyone returning during the war. But I do know that in the aftermath of the Dayton Agreement, those who had left were returning. Now, almost everyone has returned unless they sold out their property because there were many cases of people selling their property. But a large majority of them have returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did Serbs who returned after the war as you said, did they start returning already in the first two months after the Dayton Agreement?

utterances.speaker: ISMET CENGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Successively as they grew more confident about what I had said at the meeting, that I was guaranteeing them peace and that we were going to share the little that we had, they started returning. So in greater and greater numbers. To this day, not everyone has returned. Many of them have been handed the keys to their apartments and houses, but have not returned yet, and these houses stand empty. In the advertisements, there are many houses and apartments on sale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. May I - unless this question has raised any need to put further questions to the witness - may I invite you not to -- not say to empty your pockets, but at least to provide the Chamber with the newspaper articles, the clippings, you have in order to have them copied during the break. I'll take care that the originals will be returned to you. And then I'd like to give copies to the parties so that the parties can consider whether it's of any use to ask you to stay and answer any questions in relation to those newspaper clippings. I take it, Mr. Registrar, that this message will be conveyed to the victims and witness section so that they're aware of the situation. Yes. Could I ask you -- yes, please, Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, after I had left the courtroom, I was thinking about a recording that I had heard but not thought about. It refers to the territory of the Rajlovac Municipality as it was supposed to be. And I tried to put it down on a map. When I said that it had some 20.000 inhabitants, I said it in that particular moment. But the territory has even more than 35.000 inhabitants. I drew a map using the light of a lamp in the hotel. I tried to copy this diagram having a map underneath. This meant that all the temporary capacities -- facilities, the important features would have been included in this municipality, and these are important features for the entire Sarajevo, not just for the Rajlovac Municipality. I did mention some of these features to the Right Honourable Chamber here. Actually, none of the vital companies except for maybe a couple of cinemas would have been left for Sarajevo. They would all have come under the Rajlovac Municipality, even the television. So if you're interested, I would like to show that map to you on the basis of the recording we listened to yesterday. I didn't have a chance of analysing it earlier, so I did it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that you say it was not 20.000, but it was 35.000 even. That relates to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A lot. Because these were many local communes. It would have come under the municipality. These would have been Reljevo, Rajlovac, Atovici, Brijesce Brdo, Boljakov Potok, Alipasin Most, Buca Potok, Dolac, the Alipasin Most railway station, all the factories there, the public transport company, the military industries, Zrak, the Halilovic barracks. This was the second most important venue, that is the storage place for all the companies. I have it here on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I think you gave further comment to your testimony of yesterday where you talked about the Serb Municipality of Rajlovac being established, at least in principle, by February the 22nd. And whether you were aware of that, and then you answered: "No, I was not. But if I may, I should like to comment a portion of this conversation where it is indicated that the area is not densely populated, that there are not many inhabitants living there. Now, I've heard" - you continued - "this conversation for the first time these days, but now I'm able to understand it better. The fact that they counted the population, although the number was not precise, in light of that, I can claim that there's over 20.000 inhabitants living in the area, and more than 70 per cent of them are Bosniak. The area described here includes several local communes, Reljevo, Rajlovac..." That's how you continued. I do understand that you now comment that it was more than 20.000, that it was up to 35.000, and that that area included important facilities. Is that a correct understanding of your comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think even without the map, this further specification would be sufficient. Thank you very much for your further comment. Then I'd like you to give to the usher at this moment the clippings you've brought with you in order to have them copied during the break. I think it's of no use to ask the witness to remain in the building at this very moment because you might not have an opportunity to read -- to read through it all. So therefore, could -- if one of the parties would find any specific issue, and it should be an important one, not just a small one, but a relevant issue which the Chamber should hear, could I ask the parties then to inform the victims and witness section first thing tomorrow morning so that you have time this evening to go through the material and to see whether there's any need to put further questions to the witness. So Madam usher, if you could please -- perhaps we first return the original of the newspaper provided. I take it, Mr. Stewart, that the additional pages copied are not -- will not be tendered into evidence, so we just have I think it's 390 -- it's 388, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay, that's clear. So only the selected portion. That means the part is tendered into evidence. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From a procedural point of view, Your Honour, I'm wondering whether if we review these materials Mr. Cengic at some point in time needs to go home, and will he come back into court and will he be then formally excused from his completed testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what I'd like to do I is provisionally excuse Mr. Cengic from this Court and ask him to be available if he gets a message tomorrow morning to return to this Court, if asked to do so and the parties are therefore invited to inform the victims and witness section whether they would like to put additional questions to Mr. Cengic. Of course, we can never exclude that reading the newspaper articles would cause the parties to do any further investigations. If that would lead to a situation that Mr. Cengic, who then perhaps already has left, would be required to return, then the Chamber would like to know first of all what the compelling reason is to ask further questions on the basis of those newspaper articles. That's what is in the mind of the Chamber at this moment. If this would be a procedure on which the parties would like to comment, they have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To be perfectly clear, when the parties agree that Mr. Cengic's testimony is no longer required, then he's -- based on that agreement excused from further Court appearances? Does that formally end his court appearance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll tell Mr. Cengic what his situation is. And then if that leaves any questions, you can put them. Mr. Cengic, you have answered all the questions put to you by the parties, by the Bench. You have surprised us with some new material which, of course, the parties will have to look at. As it stands now, the parties will look at this material this evening, and then decide whether it would be of any use to ask additional questions to you in relation to that material. I invited the parties at the latest to inform the victims and witness section who accompanies you, more or less, to inform them by tomorrow morning. If you do not hear anything from the victims and witness unit that would require you to return into this courtroom by tomorrow in the afternoon, you're excused. That means, you're free to go. This does not for the full hundred per cent exclude that, upon more precise inspection of that material, the need might be felt by one of the parties to ask the Court's permission to recall you, to call you again to appear in The Hague. So therefore, even if you don't get a message tomorrow that we would like to see you back at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, there is, although a small chance, that at a later stage you might be needed again. So for the time being, you're excused. I thank you very much for coming. If I would not see you again tomorrow in the afternoon, I'd like to thank you very much for having come this far away. I'd like to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony you've given in this Court, at least for the next 24 hours. And I'm addressing now the parties. I think it would be -- if there's no reason to assume that Mr. Cengic will return, that to oblige him not to speak with anyone even after these 24 hours. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I only dilemma is if Mr. Cengic is no longer required to testify before this Court, normally the prohibition of having a contact with a Prosecutor ends and I would like to say thank you to Mr. Cengic at the conclusion of the day. If we notify him in the morning, that his testimony is no longer required, and if there is a 24 hour prohibition, Mr. Cengic may be on a plane before I can say thank you for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, Mr. Cengic, you now heard that the Prosecution would like to thank you for having responded to their call to appear as a witness in this Court. If that would do, Mr. Harmon, if that would solve the matter, otherwise I would invite Mr. Stewart to ask whether until tomorrow morning 10.00 would do. If the witness will not appear again --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that seems perfectly suitable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon [sic], you are supposed not to talk to anyone about your testimony until tomorrow morning 10.00. If you receive a message that the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the afternoon, then you still should not speak with anyone about your testimony. But if you do not receive any message at all, then on from 10.00 tomorrow morning, you're free, although I do not advise you to discuss in full-length your testimony given in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd only like to correct the record, Your Honour. On line 10 at page 62, it says "Mr. Harmon, you are supposed not to talk to anybody about your testimony..." Whereas the record should say Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what I said. I take it that it should say Mr. Cengic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I oppose that correction, Your Honour, because I want to cross-examine him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Cengic, therefore, wait until tomorrow morning 10.00. Thank you again if we do not see you again. If you would come back, I would thank you again after the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much. Madam usher, would you please escort --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more thing. I have some of the material here with me, and other materials are in the hotel. I would not wish to assess by myself the relevance of all these materials. I would like to hand over everything that I have with me here in The Hague. The hotel is not very far away from here. The driver could perhaps take the papers and that way the thing could be done the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a lot of material, Mr. Cengic? How much is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will make a selection of a sort, of course. There are maybe some 10 more articles here with me. But of course, I have a stack this high of documentation at home because I have the documentation relating to the entire wartime period. But it's not here with me. I've just taken some of the things that I thought might be useful. So I will make a selection of a sort, and then send the rest through the driver. Maybe some ten articles or so. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cengic, I would rather not ask you to make a selection because that -- whatever material you have with you at this moment, I would invite you to give that to Madam usher to be copied. I take it you have taken with you what you consider to be most relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's all newspaper articles, all public source. So I'd rather leave it to that, and that will then be distributed to the parties and the originals will be returned to you. Just leave it to the material with you at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just wonder in light of Your Honour's observation, it may very well be, and it might be as well to ask the witness so we're clear before he leaves that it isn't all newspaper articles, that it's actually a mixture of different types of material. It might be better to clarify that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other material than newspaper clippings, Mr. Cengic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, mostly newspaper articles. I'm referring to the material I have here. There's just maybe two or three of them that are not newspaper articles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What are they, if they are not newspaper articles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a brochure of the Novi Grad Municipality talking about the structure of the municipality, and that wouldn't be of relevance to you. And then I have some statistics as to the number of those who were killed during the war, the number of houses wrecked, damaged, and so on and so forth. This is basically an official document containing a current map of the municipality, the structure of the government up until the elections and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would invite you to provide the newspaper articles and not the other documents you just mentioned to Madam usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam usher, could you escort Mr. Cengic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have one other article that the usher passed me that was provided by Mr. Cengic. So I'll just pass that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that that could be copied as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If this is an appropriate time to discuss very briefly the issue of the interpretation, I can describe what solutions we propose, and the Court can make a decision it deems appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I had a conversation with the head of the language service section for the booths, and we talked about this issue last night and this morning. What has been agreed on for the time being and is proposed is that the language assistants in the booth would have a transcript of the intercept and would read that at a normal pace rather than trying to compress the reading into the time allotted for the actual playing of the intercept, which means that they would read from the transcript only. It would not be an interpretation. It would overlap most likely the conclusion of the tape-recorded statement. A second interpreter in the booth would be listening to the actual tape itself, and to the extent that there are significant corrections that have to be made in the transcript that has been provided, the language booth will notify the parties as to where those significant changes are, and we will bring these changes to the Court's attention if we deem them to be relevant. That's the proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's one other aspect to the proposal, Your Honour, and that is this: That the language assistants would read the speaker. So if the intercept is between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic, it might say Karadzic, and then they would read, Krajisnik, and that way the record would be more complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we agree completely with that. Just to clarify, we suppose that while the interpreters are reading at the normal pace so it can all be properly taken down, that nevertheless the actual tape will be played, won't it? Because Ms. Cmeric and Mr. Krajisnik would like to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, the tape will be played. Both the parties from the Defence will have an opportunity to listen to it, as will all people in the booth have an opportunity to listen to it. And as I say, if they find that it is necessary to augment what is the written transcript that's been read by the people in the booth, they'll notify us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So if I then well understand you, what we'll then have at the end is an audiorecording of the B/C/S text which is played, which is the part of the audiorecording of this trial. We'll then have an English text which is, as a matter of fact, the translation of the transcript of the B/C/S transcript of that intercept and which is subject to amendments if the English transcript does not fully reflect the translation of the original B/C/S spoken words. And then finally, we'll have a French translation which is a translation of the English text spoken by the interpreters on the basis of the B/C/S transcript. So the English interpreters translate the B/C/S transcript rather than the original spoken B/C/S words. And I also do understand that in the English booth, one of the interpreters will then translate the B/C/S transcript, whereas the other interpreter will not read but will follow the words spoken in B/C/S in order to identify any significant difference between the transcript and especially the English translation of the transcript and the words spoken in B/C/S. Is that a proper understanding of your suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber adopts your suggestion, Mr. Harmon, and the parties -- and not only the parties but also the interpreters and those who are responsible for the interpretation in this Court are -- deserve a lot of thanks for thinking with the parties and the Chamber to resolve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will tomorrow, Your Honour, submit to the Court one intercept where we have -- we talked about that yesterday where there was a break, and there was the addition of the word "fantastic." I've had that looked at by language assistants in my office. We have a now-revised text. I will submit that. And indeed, on that intercept there was a break, and I will confirm that and make a suggestion tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After the break, Mr. Harmon, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is -- no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Boro Bjelobrk, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, it is. Then we'll adjourn until 5 minutes past 6.00, but not until Mr. Registrar has guided us through all the exhibits, if at least the tape still allows us to do so. Yes, Mr. Registrar, could you please read for us the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit P382, map of Sarajevo; Prosecution Exhibit P383, 1991 consensus [sic] data for Bosnia; Prosecution Exhibit P384, minutes from the meetings of the citizens of the local commune Rajlovac held on 16 July 1991; Prosecution Exhibit P385 are the excerpts from the minutes of the citizens' meeting in Zabrdje, Smiljevici on 2nd July 1991; Prosecution Exhibit P386 is a map of Rajlovac Zabrdje local commune with a legend; the legend of the map will be Prosecution Exhibit P386.1; and B/C/S of the legend will be Prosecution Exhibit P386.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to change that numbering and to make it P386.A for the legend and P386.A.1 for the translation into English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, it has been carried out. Prosecution Exhibit P387, the results of the survey in Rajlovac local commune on separation; Prosecution Exhibit P388, the article "What to do with Sarajevo" by Ankica Posavljak from the Novogradsko Oko, first issue, Sarajevo, February 1992; Prosecution Exhibit P389.A is the binder containing 11 intercepts authenticated by the witness Ismet Cengic; P389.A.1 1 would be the English translation of the same; Prosecution Exhibit P389B is a CD-ROM of 11 intercepts authenticated by Mr. Ismet Cengic; Prosecution Exhibit P390 is a letter from the SDS committee members's club from the municipality Novi Grad Sarajevo dated 27 December 1991; and Prosecution Exhibit P391 is a letter from the Municipal Assembly Novi Grad Sarajevo, group committee members of 23rd December 1991 to the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we have one Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As far as Defence Exhibits, Your Honours, Defence Exhibit D32 is a newspaper article from Glas Srpska, 23rd January, 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then could the description of P388 be changed in "What to do with Zabrdje," rather than Sarajevo. And then 388 is the front page of Novogradsko Oko, and page 6 on which this appears. This is just to clarify because we have had other pages of that same newspaper in front of us which are not tendered into evidence. So it's just page -- the front page and page 6. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on line 8, page 68, the description of the exhibit is erroneously recorded. It should be census data and not consensus data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then census with a C rather than an S. Having dealt with it, we'll adjourn until 10 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just for the record, I state that you're now appearing for the Prosecution, and you're ready to call your next witness which will be Mr. Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam usher, would you please escort Mr. Bjelobrk into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bjelobrk. Before you give evidence in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And the text is now handed out to you by Madam usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated, Mr. Bjelobrk. You will first be examined by Mr. Hannis, counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, can we begin by having you state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Boro Bjelobrk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I intend to employ Rule 89F with this witness, so I would like to begin by having his ICTY statement marked as an exhibit and handing him the B/C/S version of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecution Exhibit P392.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, do you have a copy of that in front of you? Not yet, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We're going to hand you an official copy. Do you recognise that as a copy of a statement you made to OTP personnel relating to this case?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to review it before coming to Court today? The difference with that statement being that certain portions of your original statement were deleted by me for purposes of your testimony today. Apart from that, can you confirm that that is your statement and your evidence in this case?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: I confirm that this is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in addition to that statement, in preparation for your testimony today, did you have an opportunity to listen to a number of tape recorded intercepted telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: I confirm that I did have an opportunity of doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you able to identify a number of those speakers where you were able to do so and comment on the contents of certain of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. I did recognise the speakers, and I provided you with some comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just remark that Mr. Hannis did ask the witness whether he had a chance to review his statement before coming to Court today. It was perfectly normal question to ask. But it doesn't appear from the transcript that the witness actually did answer that question. He was asked: "And did you have a chance to review it before coming to Court today?" And then he went on. The answer, Your Honours, is a barely there one. It might be better for the record to be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that you confirmed that this was your statement, you did not answer yet the question whether you had an opportunity to review that statement during the last few days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have the opportunity of reading the statement, and I do confirm that it is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, counsel and Your Honour. The next item I would like to have marked and shown to the witness is an intercept authentication record. If we could give that the next number and show it to him, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P393, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, do you recognise that as a document you were able to look at which contains a record of those conversations where you were able to identify certain of the speakers and your comments about the contents of some of those conversations that you listened to?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes. This document includes what I said in view of the conversations that I had the opportunity of hearing, and I confirmed this by my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And initialled the other two pages as well?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would propose to read the Rule 89F summary of this witness if that's agreeable to counsel and the Court. I know we've done it sometimes at the beginning of a witness's testimony and sometimes at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you'd better do it at the beginning so we know what's the starting point for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I noticed but that's a very technical issue that Mr. Hannis asked whether the witness had had a chance, then I asked him whether he had had an opportunity, but of course neither of us asked whether he took that chance or -- I saw you hesitating. But the answer is understood to be that he has reviewed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's right. I made that comment to Ms. Cmeric, and there was -- one of our judges often used to say when counsel asked me if he'd had the opportunity, yes, then he would add after a pause that he hadn't taken the opportunity, but we assume the witness had, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw you discussing this with Ms. Cmeric. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, for right now, I'm just going to read a summary of what is in your written statement and then I will have some questions for you after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel, this witness was a member of the Social Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'll use the initials SDP where it occurs again. And was a member of the national assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this capacity, he negotiated with representatives of the SDS in respect of the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He explains the SDS national platform and his party's response to the SDS platform. The witness also relates how in 1991 the SDS was engaged in the process of establishing parallel state structures, discussing the resettlement of the population, organising Serb municipalities, and forming Serb autonomous regions. Bjelobrk describes the accused's public persona as being quite different from the way he acted in a nonpublic meeting that the witness attended as a representative of the trade unions. The witness describes Momcilo Krajisnik's role as the president of the assembly, noting that the position is a more powerful one than that of the president or speaker in other European parliaments. He describes the legislative process in existence at the time and gives examples of how the accused used his authority to promote the agenda of the SDS. The witness will comment on intercepted telephone conversations related to these and other relevant matters. Mr. Bjelobrk recounts an October 1991 meeting at the Lukavica barracks during which a JNA major offered him the opportunity to command a group of 150 people in the village of Miljevici. The witness recounts the October 1991 BiH Assembly session in which Radovan Karadzic made his infamous speech about the possible disappearance, extinction of the Muslim people, and the walkout by the SDS representatives. He describes subsequent efforts by the other legislators to reach a political solution to avoid a war. Mr. Bjelobrk describes his October 1991 visit as a representative of the assembly to inspect the Posavina front line and a related meeting with local leaders, including Radoslav Brdjanin and Predrag Radic. The witness comments on a January 1992 interview given by Krajisnik and on a March 1992 press report about the so-called variant A/variant B document. Mr. Bjelobrk also recounts a March 1992 conversation that he and another Serb had with Krajisnik in which the accused asked why they did not want to support the SDS. Krajisnik talked about Serb intellectuals not being able to live with other nationalities in the same country. His testimony is relevant to paragraphs 7, 8, 12, 17, and 19 of the indictment, and to all the counts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only comment I have on that is something maybe I should have noticed before because I had been supplied with this before by Mr. Hannis, ut for the future, because it's a bit late on this, for the future we suggest that words like "infamous" should be edited out. We occasional see a little bit of, well, I occasionally mentioned the word journalism from time to time in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart, I was surprised to hear that word to be used. I thought about taking off the "in."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That wouldn't quite did the trick, would it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Chamber has heard a lot of evidence on this Assembly meeting and there's no need, in whatever way the witness would describe, there would be no need to refer to it as infamous or famous or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take note of that, and we'll follow that in future 89F summaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, next I want to just briefly summarise partially some of your background information. I'll read this out and ask you if that's correct. You were born in Ilidza in 1949. You obtained a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering. You became a member of the communist party in 1968 which later became the Social Democratic Party, the SDP of BiH. Since 1991, you were a member of the SDP main board and currently a member of its presidency at the time of your statement. And in the 1990 elections, you were elected to the Council of Ministries and became a member of the BiH Parliament or National Assembly. And you are a Yugoslav by ethnic background. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: All of it is correct except for the detail that in 1990 I was elected to the Council of Municipalities of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that correction. Now, your statement is going to be evidence in this matter, so I just want to go to certain portions of it and ask you to explain or elaborate on a few matters. The first paragraph I have a question for you about for Court and counsel, is at paragraph 20 of your statement. There you talk about beginning in mid-1991, there were many speeches in the assembly, stating that Serbs from various regions "had to protect themselves." And you go on to say that you could see that the idea came from the top leadership of the SDS. I want to begin by asking you, first of all, what or who did you consider the top leadership in the SDS to be?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: The top of the SDS would be first of all the people who have the top positions in nominal terms, so that is the president and the members who have important positions in the state like members of the presidency, prime minister, et cetera. Also, I believe that members of parliament are important because in public, the SDS paid great attention to the role that the members of parliament from the ranks of the SDS were supposed to play.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were there others that you considered to be in the top leadership other than those who held the nominal positions that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Of course. According to the statute of that party, those are the members of its executive organs, like the main board, the presidency, et cetera. However, I believe that in terms of importance, the persons who held the positions I referred to were persons who were considered to be people of authority and perceived as such by the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in your position as a member of the assembly, did you have occasion to deal on a regular basis with the SDS representatives, the other members of the national assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Of course. The system of work in the parliament calls for constant communication starting from the official communication, if I can call it that, during the actual sessions of parliament. Then work in assembly commissions and other committees. And of course, the standard conversations taking place in the couloirs of the assembly. So this is all activity that took place within the assembly. Of course, there were also personal contacts outside the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a result of that contact with members of the SDS, the assembly members who were in the SDS, did you gain an impression of who they considered to be the most important members of the SDS or their top leaders?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: I think that without question, the highest authority was wielded by the SDS president, and in time the president of the assembly's position also gained in importance because the SDS paid great attention to the role of the representatives in the public. Members of the presidency did not have such authority in the public, although they did exercise important functions. And this would round off the circle of the people who were given much importance by the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1991 and early 1992, can you tell us who was the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: The president of the SDS was Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: The president of the assembly was Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, next, I would like to play an intercept and have this given the next exhibit number. And we propose to use the new procedure that Mr. Harmon described.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P394, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the interpreters are ready to start the first experience with the new system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, and to assist in that, I would like to direct the interpreters, Court, counsel, and the witness to the starting point. I'm not going to play the whole intercept; I'm going to play a portion. In the English, it begins on page 3, the fourth box down. Mr. Milosevic is speaking. In the B/C/S, it begins on page 2 of that document, three boxes up from the box where Mr. Milosevic is speaking. If that gives everyone a moment to find where we're starting, we'll begin playing the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note they don't have obviously the right text in front of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you, Mr. Hannis. The interpreters tell us they have not the right text in front of them. Let me just...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we could restart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Slobodan Milosevic: You just called at the right time. There, I have scribbled down some letter. Radovan Karadzic: Uh-huh. Slobodan Milosevic: There. I would address it to all that we are calling, and then I would say in the whole process of the Yugoslav crisis, neither in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Serbia, none of the decisions were made or proclaimed about the secession and independence. This is the best indication that the interest and the preference of all the people and of most of the population living in these republics is that Yugoslavia be saved as joint state of all equal people and republics, and that for its successful development the conditions be made. In that way, particularly emphasised is the responsibility of all the highest bodies of these republics to find solution for a peaceful and democratic outcome of the Yugoslav crisis. That is why I think that the agreement between the presidents of the republics and presidents of the republics' national assemblies on the most important questions about resolving the Yugoslav crisis would be a good basis for our joint initiative that in the Yugoslav bodies, the public as well as in other republican bodies in the interest of finding the solution which will be in favour of the interest for the solution which will establish the interests of all the Yugoslav people. And then I will add now because I haven't, I only started to write, to suggest that on Monday, presidents of the republics and the national assemblies, presidents meet up and I ask them to -- Radovan Karadzic: To confirm it, yes. Slobodan Milosevic: What do you think? Radovan Karadzic: To confirm. Excellent, excellent. Good. Slobodan Milosevic: Well, all right then. Radovan Karadzic: Yes. And all of them will arrive. Or maybe all of them or almost all of them. Slobodan Milosevic: Well, all of them could arrive. Only Alija might miss. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Slobodan Milosevic: Because be aware the key figure there is Krajisnik. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes, he is. Slobodan Milosevic: If Krajisnik did not arrive, then the representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina did not arrive as well. Radovan Karadzic: Yes, yes. Slobodan Milosevic: If Krajisnik arrives, I don't give a fuck if Alija did not arrive. Radovan Karadzic: You do that directly to all of them separately, address it in their name. Slobodan Milosevic: Yes, yes, in the name, in the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I ask the English booth whether there were any differences in what was heard and what was read in B/C/S? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No substantive differences that we could notice, but it was very fast and very hard to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least at this moment no differences have been identified. Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, this intercepted is dated August or July -- August of 1991. At that time in the former Republic of Yugoslavia, as I understand it, there were six republics that made up Yugoslavia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And each one of those had its own president, a republican president of each of the six?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: The constitutional orders in the republics were such that in five of these republics, the highest function was the presidency which at that time numbered three or six members. The only difference in Bosnia-Herzegovina was that unlike the other republics that had their presidents, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was governed by a collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And each of the six republics had its own republic assembly?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in terms of republic-level business, who or in which body was invested the power to deal on an equal level, republic to republic, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: This authority under the republican constitutions was vested with the presidents of the republics; that is, in the case of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the presidency. The assemblies did not have that sort of authority because earlier on you had these discussions by the presidents of the republics who were trying to find a joint solution to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, one of the previous answers confuses me a bit, the answer where the witness said the constitutional orders in the republics were such that in five of these republics, the highest function was the presidency which at that time numbered three or six members. And then a bit further in that answer, it says that Bosnia and Herzegovina was different because unlike the other republics that had their presidents, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was governed by a collective body. I would consider a body consisting of three or six people as a collective body. So I have difficulties understanding this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bjelobrk, did you understand what the Judge said and can you help resolve that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Of course. Out of the six Yugoslav Republics under the constitutional provisions of these republics, the five republics, namely, Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia, had presidents, whereas the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had the presidency, and that was the difference compared to the other republics that I was mentioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was three to six members, the presidency? I even did hear that you had answered, but not loud enough for the interpreters to translate it. Your answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, now I need to ask a question because I may be a little confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the five republics other than Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was an individual president in each of those five republics?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, you had a collective presidency?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the intercept you just listened to where Mr. Milosevic seemed to be arranging some kind of meeting at which he was going to invite the presidents from the six republics as well as the presidents of the national assemblies of those six republics to a meeting, did you see any significance in that particular list of invitees?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Prior to the 7th of August, these discussions aimed at finding the solution to the Yugoslav crisis were carried on by the presidents of the republics. Now, this conversation proposes that presidents of the assemblies be also involved in these discussions. We had such an initiative before on the agenda in the assembly, and some of us thought that the introduction of the presidency of the assembly into the discussions was an attempt after the failed session of the assembly in the summer of 1991, which failed primarily due to the president of the assembly who obviously gained in authority, and Milosevic was keeping this option in mind and wanted to have this option set aside as a reserve option for the speaking up of the mind of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the solution to the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to -- I started asking you about paragraph 20 and the Serb speeches about having to protect themselves, your statement that the idea -- you could see the idea came from the top leadership of the SDS. How could you see or what led you to conclude that that's where this idea came from?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: First of all, the general mood in the spring and in mid-1991 was such that there were no significant incidents calling for any sort of protection. Secondly, we had heard of these ideas for establishing some regional forms of government. And interestingly enough, they were formulated in Romanija in Eastern Herzegovina and Krajina where the Serb population is in the majority. And obviously, therefore, this system, this mechanism of protection was being formed in the areas where the Serbs were a majority, where the SDS was. Now, if you wanted to create a system of protection, it would be logical to create it in the areas where a certain ethnicity is in a minority in relation to the others. However, time will show later on that this was a practice applied by the SDS until the formation of the assembly of the Serbian people and until the anti-constitutional takeovers started taking place there. In my opinion, this was an idea developed by the leadership, first of all, because the common citizens on the ground did not have any special purposes for protection. And secondly, as you will see from one of the transcripts here, that the drawing of the map in this sense was being done by a very narrow circle of the people -- from among the leadership of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Also in paragraph 20, you talk about -- or you say: "The process of regional organisation and protection progressed from this grouping of municipalities in Romanija and the creation of SAO, Serb Autonomous Regions in Herzegovina and Krajina, et cetera, all the way through to the establishment of the Republika Srpska." And you end by concluding that this was "very well organised and was a progressive strategy aimed toward the ultimate conclusion of national separation." What led you to that conclusion? What did you base that conclusion on?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: There are several elements that would logically point to such a conclusion to any active participant in the events. First of all, the development of the SDS policy through the assembly and municipal bodies was in a way defensive. They were formulating their responses to the initiatives of others, and they merely had to the need to respond to that in defence. When the crisis was on the table already, people were trying to find compromise. And typically for them, they were trying to find a compromise through this defensive policy. Secondly, in 1991, there was a thesis according to which each ethnicity will have its own government and run its own government, which means that you will have government mechanisms in individual areas, and you will separate the ethnicities along these lines. There were no problems in the areas where the three ethnicities could reach an agreement. However, wherever they could not, that's where the problems arose. That's where the SDS professed that their position was the position of the Serbian people. Now, when we're talking about the grouping of municipalities along this SAO regionalisation policy and in view of the fact that the assembly proclaimed to have a legitimate majority in the areas where the population was predominant, this was a process lasting for some 10, 11 months. And you could see the way this -- the issue of the majority areas progressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. Now, in paragraphs 21 to 25, and also in paragraph 50 of your statement, you discuss in some detail how, in your view, Mr. Krajisnik used his authority as president of the BiH Assembly to actually obstruct the functioning of that body. And in paragraph 22, you describe an example of that related to a particular proposal that you and your party wanted to get on the assembly agenda. First of all, can I ask you, do you recall what was that proposal that you were seeking to get on the assembly agenda?

utterances.speaker: BORO BJELOBRK
utterances.text: Prompted by the failed negotiations in Split where all the presidents of the republics tried to reach an agreement, the Social Democratic Party, that is, its representatives, came out with the proposal to find a solution for Bosnia-Herzegovina within the entire crisis, and there were two aspects of the proposal. First of all, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should be placed in an equidistance in relation to Serbia and Croatia. In view of the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was composed by people of Serbian, Croat, and Bosniak ethnicities, it would be unnatural and unrealistic to seek for a solution that would not create a symmetrical type of relationship vis-a-vis Croatia and vis-a-vis Serbia. The second aspect was the securing of human rights, not only ethnic rights of all the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was the basis of this platform that had some other points as well. We put forth this proposal to the assembly. From the ranks of the SDS representatives, we met with opposition as early as -- at the point of the adoption of the agenda. Mr. Krajisnik voted for the item to be inserted into the agenda, and it was at this particular session that the SDS representative walked out of the session. In order to have such a proposal adopted, we needed some 120 or 121 votes, which made up 51 per cent. We lacked one vote, and the key vote that was lacking because of which our platform was not adopted was Mr. Krajisnik's who opposed the idea. I have to admit that he implemented the whole procedure in a fully democratic way. However, if the SDS stance was to even walk out of the session rather than vote on that platform, he did not do that. He stayed there. For us, it was normal to at least expect some sort of a debate. The only thing that happened was that we basically lacked one vote. And in general, any idea that was not of -- that was not to the liking of the SDS representatives would be met either with the walkout of the SDS representatives or with the obstruction by Mr. Krajisnik at the end of the entire procedure. And this happened regardless of the topic, be it the number of intervals to be taken during a session or be it other topics that -- like, for instance, the voting system that would manage to circumvent the obstruction by the SDS representatives. As it was, we had the sessions either interrupted or we had the walkout of the SDS representatives. Finally, when there was some hope of the assembly being able to vote for proposal, the SDS representatives said that only those items could be placed on the agenda where consensus would be achieved by all the three ethnicities, and the second proposal was that 51 per cent of the vote was not going to be enough for a proposal to be adopted because one ethnicity was, in their words, too loud. In the end, all this meant that the work of the assembly had to be obstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be a good time for me to break if it's not too early.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not too early. Mr. Bjelobrk, we'll adjourn for the day. I'd like you to return tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in this same courtroom. I, however, have to tell you that there's a -- although small chance that we would have to do another thing first, the chance is small, as I said, but it's still there, and I just wanted to let you know in advance. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given today and you're still about to give in this Court. Madam usher, may I ask you to escort Mr. Bjelobrk out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just for our information, this witness was scheduled even on the last sheet, which is of the 9th of November, 2.00, so that's rather recent, for six hours. At the same time, the -- I may take it that under Rule 89F that you have another estimate which is more realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I spoke with Mr. Stewart before I began, and I hope I can complete this witness in three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. All together. So you would say tomorrow you would need a little bit over two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then now I better understand that the parties still are confident that we can finish the witnesses scheduled for this week. We adjourn --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, just two points if I may. First of all, I'm not quite sure when we're going to be receiving material from the previous witness who was going back to conduct his search?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that it has already been copied, that it's on the corner of that table, and that you'll receive it immediately after this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two points, Your Honour. The other one is we noticed this witness has with him, we didn't bother about it just now because it was a short time and he didn't seem to be referring to it, but he did apparently have in front of him some sort of fairly thick diary or agenda. We wonder whether it can just be checked tomorrow before he goes into the witness box because he really ought not to take anything with him. We've had this before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will check on that, Your Honour. From my observation, I think it's a copy of the statement and a copy of the exhibits that were proposed to be shown to him, but I'll address that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would first advise the witness to keep that at a sufficient distance and not to be consulted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.
